tells.1: none (clunky and repetitive, like an unpolished human draft: 'You don't have to measure our pre-measured dry ingredients')
tells.2: Stacked parallel fragments ('A little measuring done. A little joy delivered.' / 'An afternoon with the oven on. Something homemade to share.')
tells.3: Mild over-smoothing; 'Plan on an afternoon...' feels like a fragment that was rewritten into a sentence
tells.4: Formulaic 'Maybe it's... Maybe it's just... Either way' rhetorical build
tells.5: Social-proof stats tacked onto the end of an anecdote ('...and we have about 2,800 active subscribers')

reason: Version 5 replaces vague mood copy with concrete, credible specifics (the recipe is included, a named mill, a real subscriber story, a subscriber count), which builds trust and reads most human. It's the one to send, provided those facts are verified before publishing. Version 3 is the best fallback.
